full_judgment:
18. In a case of this nature the prosecution is required to prove their case strictly according to the principle laid down in the Evidence Act in spite of the provision of section 4 of the Prevention or Corruption Act II of 1947. The proof required of the prosecution has been elaborately discussed in the case of M. C. Mitra Vs. The State in A.I.R. 1951 Cal. 524. The learned judge has observed thus:- 

 19. In my judgment this does not mean that the burden of proof on the prosecution to establish the acceptance of the agreement to accept or the obtaining or the agreement to obtain the gratification of the valuable thing is at all displaced by this section. The burden still remains on the prosecution and it is only when the prosecution has discharged that burden that the presumption of (a) motive or reward or (b) absence or inadequacy of consideration will be made against the accused. But not until then such presumption can operate against the accused, notwithstanding section 4 Prevention Corruption Act, 1947. The burden still remain upon the prosecution to prove first that the accused had accepted or agreed to accept or has obtained or agreed to obtain the gratification or the valuable thing and this proof must be in accordance with the standard of proof laid down by Sec.3, Evidence Act. Thus if is found that the prosecution in this particular case has not been able to prove the motive for Acceptance of the bribe. Furthermore the contradiction in the evidence of the prosecution witnesses goes to the discredit of the prosecution. It is particularly unfortunate that in a case where traps are arranged by the Police the Magistrates are involved in the trap party as a member of the trap. This practice has been disapproved by the High Courts of this country and inspite of that the prosecution thought it fit to take a Magistrate in the trap party. In this particular case it is unfortunate to find that the Magistrate's evidence on this point has been contradicted by the investigating Officer, P. W. 13.
